To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
patients with early HCC and a single lesion < 5 cm in diameter could be safely treated with LR with a 5-year survival rate of 80%.

(1) LR is a feasible option for selected patients with early and resectable tumors, with an excellent long-term outcome and a low risk of recurrence; (2) LR is associated with lower mortality and morbidity, and with shorter hospitalization than LT, and (3) LR is cost-effective compared with LT.

1) the definition of early HCC should include the presence of a single lesion ≤5 cm; 2) LR should be performed in the presence of a normal liver parenchyma; 3) in case of cirrhosis, the presence of a Child A cirrhosis and a single lesion ≤3 cm should be considered as the best selection criteria.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new and improved methods for the treatment of cancer and other diseases, and the development of novel methods for the treatment and diagnosis of cancer.
the following questions: (i) what is the definition of early HCC? (ii) is there any subgroup in which the prognosis after LR is better than LT?
the development of a new generation of materials with improved properties.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
LR is the best option in the treatment of HCC patients who are not suitable for LT and have a small and single HCC lesion.
the best treatment for HCC is a multidisciplinary approach with a team that includes hepatologists, surgeons, radiologists and pathologists.

the best treatment for HCC patients is to be determined on the basis of a multidisciplinary evaluation of the patient's clinical condition and of the tumor features, and that the choice between LT or LR should be based on the patient's general condition, on the tumor size and the number of lesions and on the possibility of achieving a complete resection.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have identified an early HCC subgroup in which LR could represent the best curative alternative to LT.

the patients who could be candidates for primary LR should be those with a single tumor, with a maximum diameter of 5 cm, and with a Milan score of 3 points or less, and that the patients who should be candidates for primary LT should be those with more than 2 tumors, or those with 2 or less but with at least one tumor with a diameter of 5-7 cm.
we have identified a subset of patients with early HCC (≤5 cm) in whom LR is as effective as LT in terms of overall survival and recurrence-free survival.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a subgroup of early HCC patients could benefit from primary LR.
a subgroup of patients with early HCC can be safely treated with primary LR.
patients with a single HCC ≤5 cm or ≤3 HCC ≤3 cm, with no vascular invasion or extrahepatic spread, and with adequate liver function could be treated with LR with similar results to LT.
